summary.text: Quadratic reciprocity makes 5 a square modulo p, so choosing a root x and setting n=x-1 gives 3≤n

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
C_n=\frac1{\displaystyle 2-\frac3{\displaystyle 3-\frac4{\displaystyle 4-\cdots-\frac n{-4}}}}
\qquad(n\ge 3),
\]
and let \(a(n)\) be its reduced positive denominator. We prove that every prime \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\) occurs as some \(a(n)\).

We first encode the continued fraction by an integer recurrence.

For fixed \(n\ge3\), define integers \(S_k=S(n,k)\) backwards by
\[
S_n=4,\qquad S_{n-1}=5n-4,
\]
and, for \(2\le k<n-1\),
\[
S_k=kS_{k+1}-(k+1)S_{k+2}. \tag{1}
\]
All these quantities are integers by construction. If \(R_k\) denotes the tail beginning with \(k\), namely
\[
R_{n-1}=n-1+\frac n4
\]
and
\[
R_k=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}}\qquad(2\le k<n-1),
\]
then
\[
R_k=\frac{S_k}{S_{k+1}}. \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, for \(k=n-1\),
\[
R_{n-1}=n-1+\frac n4=\frac{5n-4}{4}= rac{S_{n-1}}{S_n}.
\]
If (2) holds at \(k+1\), then by (1)
\[
R_k=k-\frac{k+1}{S_{k+1}/S_{k+2}}
   =\frac{kS_{k+1}-(k+1)S_{k+2}}{S_{k+1}}
   =\frac{S_k}{S_{k+1}}.
\]
Thus the expression inside the outer reciprocal in \(C_n\) is
\[
R_2=\frac{S_2}{S_3},
\]
so \(C_n=S_3/S_2\). Consequently, \(a(n)\) is the absolute value of the reduced numerator of \(S_2/S_3\).

We next evaluate \(S_2\). Put
\[
N=n^2+2n-4.
\]
For every \(2\le k\le n-1\), one has the invariant
\[
(k-1)S_k-k(k-2)S_{k+1}=N. \tag{3}
\]
At \(k=n-1\), the left side is
\[
(n-2)(5n-4)-(n-1)(n-3)\cdot4=n^2+2n-4.
\]
Moreover, using (1),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(k-1)S_k-k(k-2)S_{k+1}\\
&=(k-1)\bigl(kS_{k+1}-(k+1)S_{k+2}\bigr)-k(k-2)S_{k+1}\\
&=kS_{k+1}-(k+1)(k-1)S_{k+2},
\end{aligned}
\]
which is the same expression with \(k\) replaced by \(k+1\). This proves (3) by backward induction. Taking \(k=2\) gives
\[
S_2=N=n^2+2n-4. \tag{4}
\]

We will also need positivity. Certainly \(S_n=4>0\), and \(N>0\) for \(n\ge3\). Rearranging (3), for \(2\le k\le n-1\), gives
\[
(k-1)S_k=N+k(k-2)S_{k+1}.
\]
Starting from \(S_n>0\) and descending in \(k\), this shows that every \(S_k\) with \(2\le k\le n\) is positive. In particular,
\[
S_3>0. \tag{5}
\]

We now prove the divisibility fact that controls exactly what is cancelled when \(S_2/S_3\) is reduced.

Define integers
\[
M_0=1,\qquad M_{d+1}=M_d+(d+1)!.
\]
Thus
\[
M_d=1+\sum_{i=1}^d i!,
\]
and \(M_d\) is even whenever \(d\ge1\): \(M_1=2\), and every subsequently added factorial is even.

For every \(d\ge0\) with \(d+3<n\), we claim
\[
2S_3-(d+3)(d+1)!S_{d+4}=M_dS_2. \tag{6}
\]
For \(d=0\), this is
\[
2S_3-3S_4=S_2,
\]
which is (3) at \(k=3\). Suppose (6) holds for \(d\). Formula (3) at \(k=d+4\) says
\[
(d+3)S_{d+4}-(d+4)(d+2)S_{d+5}=S_2.
\]
Multiplying this equation by \((d+1)!\) gives
\[
(d+3)(d+1)!S_{d+4}-(d+4)(d+2)!S_{d+5}=(d+1)!S_2.
\]
Adding this to (6) proves the formula for \(d+1\), because
\(M_{d+1}=M_d+(d+1)!\). Hence (6) follows by induction.

We record two parity properties of the recurrence. First, if \(n\) is even, every \(S_k\) is even. This follows by backward induction from
\[
S_n=4,
\qquad S_{n-1}=5n-4,
\]
which are both even, and recurrence (1). In that case write
\[
S_k=2T_k.
\]
Dividing (1) by 2 shows that the \(T_k\) obey the same recurrence,
\[
T_k=kT_{k+1}-(k+1)T_{k+2}, \tag{7}
\]
with
\[
T_n=2,
\qquad T_{n-1}=5\frac n2-2.
\]
If, in addition, \(n\ge6\), then
\[
2\mid T_k\qquad( k\le n-2). \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, from (7),
\[
T_{n-2}=(n-2)T_{n-1}-(n-1)T_n,
\]
and both terms on the right are even because \(n-2\) is even and \(T_n=2\). Next,
\[
T_{n-3}=(n-3)T_{n-2}-(n-2)T_{n-1}
\]
is even. Thereafter ordinary backward induction in (7) applies: once \(T_{k+1}\) and \(T_{k+2}\) are even, so is \(T_k\). This proves (8).

Now suppose that \(p\) is prime, \(n<p\), and
\[
N=n^2+2n-4=kp \tag{9}
\]
for a positive integer \(k\). We prove
\[
k\mid S_3. \tag{10}
\]

First consider the main range
\[
3\le k\le n-3.
\]
Set \(d=k-3\) in (6). Since \(S_2=kp\), this gives
\[
2S_3-k(k-2)!S_{k+1}=M_{k-3}kp. \tag{11}
\]
If \(k\) is odd, (11) says \(k\mid2S_3\), and \(k\) is coprime to 2, so \(k\mid S_3\).

Suppose instead that \(k\) is even, say \(k=2r\). Equation (9) then implies that \(n\) is even: modulo 2,
\[
n^2+2n-4\equiv n^2\equiv n\pmod2,
\]
while \(kp\) is even. Thus all \(S_j\) are even, and we may write \(S_j=2T_j\). Also, since \(k\ge3\) is even, \(k\ge4\), so \(k-3\ge1\); hence \(M_{k-3}=2M'\) for some integer \(M'\). Substitution into (11) yields
\[
4T_3-4r(k-2)!T_{k+1}=4rM'p.
\]
After division by 4,
\[
T_3=r\bigl((k-2)!T_{k+1}+M'p\bigr).
\]
Therefore
\[
S_3=2T_3=2r\bigl((k-2)!T_{k+1}+M'p\bigr),
\]
which is divisible by \(2r=k\). This proves (10) in the main range.

It remains to handle cofactors outside that range. We first establish a useful size reduction. Because \(n<p\), we have \(p\ge n+1\). Also
\[
kp=N<(n+1)^2.
\]
Consequently \(k<n+1\), for otherwise \(kp\ge(n+1)^2\). If \(k>n-3\), it follows that
\[
k\in\{n-2,n-1,n\}.
\]
If \(k=n-2\), then
\[
N=n^2+2n-4=(n-2)(n+4)+4.
\]
Since \(k\mid N\), this implies \(k\mid4\).

If \(k=n-1\), then \(p\ge n+3\) is impossible, since it would give
\[
kp\ge(n-1)(n+3)=n^2+2n-3>N.
\]
Thus, because \(p>n\), either \(p=n+1\) or \(p=n+2\). The first choice would give
\[
(n-1)(n+1)=n^2-1=n^2+2n-4,
\]
so \(2n=3\), impossible. The second would give
\[
(n-1)(n+2)=n^2+n-2=n^2+2n-4,
\]
so \(n=2\), contrary to \(n\ge3\). Hence this case cannot occur.

If \(k=n\), then \(p\ge n+2\) would imply
\[
kp\ge n(n+2)=n^2+2n>N.
\]
Therefore \(p=n+1\), and (9) becomes
\[
n(n+1)=n^2+2n-4,
\]
so \(n=4\). Thus \(k=4\), and again \(k\mid4\).

We have proved that if \(k\) is not at most \(n-3\), then \(k\mid4\). If instead \(k\le n-3\) but \(k<3\), positivity leaves only \(k=1\) or \(k=2\), both of which also divide 4. Hence, outside the main range, necessarily
\[
k\in\{1,2,4\}.
\]
For \(k=1\), (10) is immediate.

The case \(k=2\) is actually impossible under the prime congruences that will concern us. Indeed, as noted above, even \(k\) forces even \(n\); write \(n=2m\). Equation (9) then gives
\[
4m^2+4m-4=2p,
\]
or
\[
p=2(m^2+m-1).
\]
Thus the prime \(p\) is even, so \(p=2\), contrary to \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\).

Finally suppose \(k=4\). Again \(n\) is even. A prime congruent to 1 or 9 modulo 10 is at least 11, so (9) gives \(N=4p\ge44\), and therefore
\[
n^2+2n=N+4\ge48.
\]
This forces \(n\ge6\). Property (8), applied at \(k=3\), says that \(T_3\) is even. Since \(S_3=2T_3\), we obtain \(4\mid S_3\), as required. This completes the proof of (10) in every case relevant to us.

We need one more fact: although the cofactor \(k\) divides \(S_3\), the prime \(p\) does not. More precisely, under the assumptions above and with \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\),
\[
p\nmid S_3. \tag{12}
\]
Certainly \(p\mid S_2\) by (4) and (9). Suppose also that \(p\mid S_3\). We show inductively that \(p\mid S_j\) for every \(2\le j\le n\). Assume this has been proved through \(S_{j-1}\), where \(j\ge4\). Recurrence (1), used at index \(j-2\), says
\[
S_{j-2}=(j-2)S_{j-1}-(j-1)S_j.
\]
The first two displayed terms are divisible by \(p\), so \(p\mid(j-1)S_j\). But
\[
1\le j-1<n<p,
\]
so the prime \(p\) does not divide \(j-1\). Euclid's lemma therefore gives \(p\mid S_j\). Induction reaches \(S_n=4\), so \(p\mid4\). On the other hand, a prime congruent to 1 or 9 modulo 10 is neither 2 nor 5 and is in fact at least 11: in the residue class 1 the first possible prime is 11, while in the residue class 9 the only smaller positive candidate is 9, which is not prime. Thus \(p\mid4\) is impossible. This proves (12).

We now construct the required index \(n\) for a given prime \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\).

First, 5 is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\). Indeed, \(p\ne2,5\), and since \(5\equiv1\pmod4\), quadratic reciprocity gives
\[
\left(\frac5p\right)=\left(\frac p5\right).
\]
Our assumption implies
\[
p\equiv1\quad\text{or}\quad4\pmod5.
\]
Both 1 and 4 are nonzero squares modulo 5, so \((p/5)=1\), and hence \((5/p)=1\). Choose a residue \(x\), represented by an integer with
\[
0\le x<p,
\]
such that
\[
x^2\equiv5\pmod p. \tag{13}
\]
As above, \(p\ge11\). The representative \(x\) cannot be \(0,1,2\), or 3. For these values, \(x^2-5\) is respectively \(-5,-4,-1,4\), none divisible by a prime at least 11. Therefore
\[
4\le x<p.
\]
Set
\[
n=x-1.
\]
Then
\[
3\le n<p,
\]
and (13) gives
\[
p\mid x^2-5=(n+1)^2-5=n^2+2n-4=N. \tag{14}
\]
Write
\[
N=kp
\]
with \(k\in\mathbb N\). Since \(N>0\), we have \(k>0\).

By (10), \(k\mid S_3\); write
\[
S_3=kQ
\]
for an integer \(Q\). Positivity of \(S_3\) and of \(k\) gives \(Q>0\). By (12), \(p\nmid S_3\). In particular \(p\nmid Q\), since \(p\mid Q\) would imply \(p\mid kQ=S_3\). As \(p\) is prime, this means
\[
\gcd(p,Q)=1. \tag{15}
\]
Using \(S_2=kp\), we now have
\[
R_2=\frac{S_2}{S_3}=\frac{kp}{kQ}=\frac pQ.
\]
By (15), this is already in lowest terms, with positive numerator and denominator. Therefore
\[
C_n=\frac1{R_2}=\frac Qp
\]
is also in lowest terms, and its reduced denominator is exactly \(p\). Hence
\[
a(n)=p.
\]

Since the construction applies to every prime \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\), every such prime occurs in A363347, as claimed.
